paper_title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly solve multi-step tasks by interacting with an environment (Yao et al., 2023), and external memory allows them to improve from experience without updating their parameters (Sumers et al., 2024; Hu *Equal contribution; Equal advising. 1 Figure 1: Memory-induced degradation and WikiTrace. (a) The agent solves task without memory but fails with memory that holds wrong insight. (b) With WikiTrace, the agent follows the wrong insights links to its source run, revises it, and solves the task. et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2026). Specifically, memory distills trajectories of past tasks, namely their sequences of actions and observations, into concise lessons that are reused on new tasks, allowing the agent to avoid repeated exploration and to follow procedures specific to its environment. Prior work captures such lessons in diverse forms, including verbal reflections, executable skills, instruction manuals, workflows, and reasoning strategies (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). However, memory does not always help and can even lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory (Zhang et al., 2026a; Xiong et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026a) (Figure 1a). Reliable experience reuse therefore requires solving more tasks while preserving those the agent already solves, but average accuracy cannot tell the two apart. We thus measure them separately, as Gain, the rate at which memory turns failures into successes, and Regression, the rate at which it turns successes into failures. As shown in Figure 5, existing memory methods exhibit Regression comparable to, or even higher than, that of rerunning the agent without memory. To understand this degradation, we analyze tasks that the agent consistently solves without memory but fails with it, and find that 52% of the failures trace to memory item the agent followed (Figure 3), most often wrong one. Wrong items arise because trajectory comes with only single label, success or failure, which does not reveal which of its many actions caused that outcome. Any method that learns lessons from such trajectory therefore has to guess which actions matter and under which conditions, and each wrong guess yields lesson that misleads the agent on new tasks. Yet, existing approaches provide lessons without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them, even though the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson often remains in that trajectory. To this end, we present WikiTrace, an evidencelinked memory system that keeps each lesson together with path back to its original trajectory (Figures 1b and 2), combining the strengths of both: lesson concisely tells the agent what to do, whereas the trajectory faithfully records what actually happened but is too long to reread for every decision. Specifically, WikiTrace organizes its memory into three layers linked from top to bottom: each lesson is stored as concise insight, which links down to compilation that summarizes why its trajectory succeeded or failed, and further down to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever an insight lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from failed trajectory, descends through its links with terminal tools to recover missing details or revise the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks comprising eight suites, spanning simulated text worlds (Shridhar et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Dagan et al., 2025) and tool-use environments (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2026; Trivedi et al., 2024). WikiTrace achieves the best performance on every suite, improving over the agent without memory by 10.7 points on average and outperforming baseline given the same insights alone by 3.2 points, while reducing memory-induced degradation (Regression from 6.5% to 4.5%). Further analyses show that the agent consults the linked evidence more often on harder tasks, where its advantage is largest, and gains most when the evidence changes its plan. These gains hold under another backbone.

sections.title: 2.1 Experience-Driven Procedural Memory
sections.content: Language agents increasingly convert past execution experience into procedural memory that can guide future decisions. Prior methods retain verbal feedback or successful trajectories (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024), accumulate executable skills (Wang et al., 2024), or distill experience into reusable guidelines, manuals, workflows, modular procedures, and multigranular scripts (Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026). Continual approaches further update reasoning memories and playbooks with new successful and failed experience (Zhou et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Cao et al., 2026). These approaches develop mechanisms for distilling, selecting, and updating experience for reuse. WikiTrace focuses on reassessing the resulting guidance during task execution, linking each lesson to its source evidence so that the agent can examine its basis and applicability to the current task.

sections.title: 2.2 Reliable Reuse of Unverified Memory
sections.content: Reusing past experience does not always improve an agents performance. Agents ignore or misinterpret relevant condensed experience (Zhao et al., 2026a), encounter retrieval competition and negative transfer during continual learning (Hu et al., 2026a), and exhibit amplified unsafe behavior when reusing execution-oriented experience collected from benign tasks (Zhao et al., 2026c). These findings motivate evaluating the failures introduced by memory alongside the tasks it helps solve. We explicitly separate Gain from Regression to highlight memory-induced degradation that aggregate accuracy obscures. Research on memory admission and revision addresses reliability by controlling which experiences and lessons are retained. PREPING validates synthetic practice trajectories before storage (Choi et al., 2026), SkillOpt admits skill updates through held-out evaluation (Yang et al., 2026), and ReMe updates or removes memories using subsequent utility (Cao et al., 2026). WikiTrace complements these approaches by focusing on how stored lessons inform decisions during task execution. This perspective treats reliable memory reuse as question of both which lessons to retain and whether those lessons are justified in the situations where they are applied. 2 Figure 2: Overview of WikiTrace. (a) compiler turns each past run into compilation, diagnosis of why the run succeeded or failed, and insights, each concise lesson. All layers stay linked. (b) Each layers documents follow fixed template. (c) The agent starts from every insight and descends through the links under the conditions shown.

sections.title: 2.3 Memory Structure and Access
sections.content: Agent memory design concerns both how past experience is organized and how agents access it during task execution. Hierarchical approaches organize experience at multiple levels of detail for compression, planning, and retrieval (Hu et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026b), while HORMA connects filesystem summaries to raw interaction history and learns to select minimal sufficient context (Hsu et al., 2026). Beyond memory organization, active-access methods determine when and what to retrieve during reasoning (Zhang et al., 2026c; Zhao et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2026). Direct Corpus Interaction (DCI) provides general approach to corpus access through terminal tools (Li et al., 2026). WikiTrace brings these two concerns together around the reassessment of procedural lessons: its structure preserves the connection between lesson and its source execution, and its access mechanism lets the agent consult that execution when deciding how to apply the lesson.

sections.title: 3 WikiTrace
sections.content: We first define the problem setting and examine memory-induced degradation to motivate WikiTrace. We then describe its memory construction and test-time evidence access (Figure 2).

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Setting
sections.content: We consider an agent that reuses fixed corpus of past runs collected without memory, Dtrain = {(xi, ri, si)}N i=1. Each run consists of task xi, trajectory ri recording the agents actions and observations, and binary outcome si {0, 1} indicating task success or failure. No gold solutions or expert explanations are available, so runs outcome does not exactly tell us why it succeeded or failed. Thus, an insight drawn from it is not always valid. We construct memory from this corpus before any test task runs, with no additional run to validate an individual memory item. Once constructed, the memory remains fixed and read-only for an agent solving new tasks. Our objective is to improve task performance through experience reuse while limiting memory-induced degradation on tasks the agent solves without memory.

Each insight is separate document that says what to do, when it applies, which run it came from, and whether that run succeeded. sections.title: 3.3 Constructing Source-Linked Memory
sections.content: WikiTrace constructs memory = (R, C, I, E), consisting of raw trajectories R, compilations C, insights I, and source links E. Each run is processed independently so that every extracted lesson remains connected to the experience it came from. Compilation and insight extraction compiler reads task xi, the agents trajectory ri on that task, and binary signal si of its success or failure, producing compilation ci and set of insights Ii: (ci, Ii) = Compiler(xi, ri, si).

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks We evaluate on eight suites across five benchmarks. Three are simulated text worlds, where the agent issues one text command at time: ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) (household tasks), ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) (science experiments) and PlanCraft (Dagan et al., 2025) (Minecraft crafting). Two are tool-use environments: AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) poses everydashed line shows this rerun baseline, measuring outcome changes without memory. WikiTrace achieves Regression of 4.5%, compared with 6.5% for Insights Only and 9.7% for the rerun baseline. Its Regression is lower than Insights Only on seven of the eight suites, and it is the only method whose Regression confidence interval lies entirely below the rerun band. This reduction accompanies higher Gain: WikiTrace exceeds the rerun baseline by 35 percentage points, compared with 27 for Insights Only and 7 to 14 for existing memory methods. Because WikiTrace and Insights Only differ only in access to source runs, the higher Gain and lower Regression are attributable to that access. Relative to Insights Only, wrong or out-of-scope items cause half as many of WikiTraces regressions (Figure 3). Appendix provides results for individual suites.

sections.title: 5.1 When Does Descent Help?
sections.content: Insights Only gives the agent the same insights, so comparing it with WikiTrace on the same task and trial shows what access to source runs adds. We split WikiTraces test runs in the three textworld benchmarks into Descent runs, which open compilation or raw trajectory, and Stay runs, which do not (Figure 6). WikiTrace descends more often on harder tasks, in 22% of runs on Easy tasks and 44% on Hard ones. Descent runs lead Insights Only by 1.6 to 4.7 points more than Stay runs at every difficulty and on every benchmark. The gap between Descent and Stay grows with difficulty, from 1.8 points on Easy tasks to 3.7 on Medium and 4.1 on Hard ones. These results suggest that source runs help more on harder tasks. The agent chooses when to descend, however, so Descent and Stay runs differ in more than the descent. Stay runs also lead Insights Only, by 0.6 to 12.4 points. In Stay runs, WikiTrace reports 19 to 28% fewer insights as used,3 which suggests more selective use of memory. The reduction is larger in Descent runs, 38 to 57%.

sections.content: Table 1 shows that WikiTrace achieves the highest performance on all eight suites, averaging 90.2 compared with 79.5 for No Memory. sections.title: 5.5 Does WikiTrace Generalize?
sections.content: WikiTrace also achieves the highest performance on all three evaluated suites with GLM-5.3-flash  (Table 2)  . We evaluate all methods on PlanCraft and ScienceWorld at medium reasoning effort, using training executions generated by the same model to construct memory. WikiTrace averages 92.7, exceeding Insights Only by 1.8 percentage points and No Memory by 21.5. Each existing memory method falls below No Memory on at least one suite. This pattern mirrors the DeepSeek results, supporting the benefit of source-linked memory across the two models.

sections.title: 5.6 Resolving Conflicting Insights
sections.content: Figure 11 illustrates how WikiTrace resolves conflicting insights by revisiting source evidence. In PlanCraft, an insight from failed run incorrectly rules out valid procedure that another recommends. The successful runs observations show that the procedure works. WikiTrace revises the insight and succeeds, whereas Insights Only, given identical insights, follows the wrong guidance and fails. This case shows how raw trajectories enable agents to reassess interpretations embedded in insights and compilations.

ALFWorld Training holds 50 games of the training split, eight or nine per task type, in rooms that also appear in valid_seen. valid-seen is the full set of 101 valid_seen games filtered to rooms visited by the 50 training games, and valid-unseen uses all 134 valid_unseen games, set in four rooms absent from training. ScienceWorld We use ten of the 30 task types, boil, melt, freeze, change-the-state-of-matter-of, use-thermometer, measure-melting-point-knownmeasure-melting-point-unknownsubstance, substance, test-conductivity, test-conductivity-ofunknown-substances, and chemistry-mix. Each meets three conditions. Its variations pose distinct tasks. Its training and test descriptions are largely disjoint. Its reference solutions fit the simulators 100step limit. Training holds five variations per type from the training split, and test holds 100 variations from the test split whose description does not occur in training. PlanCraft We use solvable examples only, weighted toward medium and hard ones. Training holds 50 examples of the training split with distinct target items that also occur in the test split. plancraft-seen holds 100 test examples whose target is training target, and plancraft-unseen 100 whose target occurs in no solvable training example. AppWorld scenario groups three tasks and is solved only when all three pass, so every suite keeps scenarios whole. We use difficulty 2 and 3 only. sections.title: Degradation
sections.content: A judge, gpt-5.6-sol at medium reasoning effort, labels every strong degradation case of Section 3.2 with the system prompt of Figure 14. The user message holds the cases files. These are the case metadata, the run with memory, the run without memory on the same task and trial, the memory as the agent saw it, and the evaluation of both runs. The judge finds the turn where the run with memory first departs from the run without memory and gives the case one of five causes. Figures 16 to 20 show one case of each cause. (A) Wrong item. The item states something false about the environment. (B) Out-of-scope item. sound item is applied outside its scope. (C) Misused item. sound item in scope is misread or stretched. (D) Missed better item. sound item is followed while memory holds better one. (E) No link to memory. No item explains the departure. 18 System prompt of the regression judge You investigate one case of memory-induced regression and return one verdict as JSON. # The case An agent ran one test task three times without memory and succeeded every time. It then ran the same task with memory and failed. Your job is to decide whether the memory caused that failure, and if so how. The user message holds the case's files, each after line "=== <file name> ===". Those lines are not part of any file. - `case.json` gives the benchmark, suite, trial, task id and how the memory reached the agent. - `memory_run.md` is the failed run with memory. header gives the task and how the episode ended, then each turn gives the agent's reasoning, its action and clipped observation. - `nomem.md` is successful run without memory on the same task and trial, in the same format. - `memory.txt` is the memory exactly as the agent saw it, up to about 110,000 characters. The memory sat in the agent's first user message, before the task. For some methods list of the most similar past runs followed the task in the same message, and `memory.txt` includes it after the memory. - `eval_memory.json` and `eval_nomem.json` record how each episode was scored. The run without memory is an independent run of the same task, not replay. Two runs can differ by chance, so difference counts as caused by memory only under the evidence rule. # Items An item is any unit of memory the agent saw: an insight, workflow, rule or memory item in `memory.txt`, past run listed there, or past run or its summary that the agent opened during the episode. Cite an item by its id, for example `Workflow 3`, `Memory Item 2`, ` insight-0039`, `4.`, `[si-00012]` or `step-0016`. # Evidence rule Memory caused the divergence only if at least one of these holds. - e1. The agent's reasoning in the memory run refers to an item, by id, by title or by close paraphrase. - e2. The agent's actions follow steps an item prescribes and depart from what the run without memory did at that point. An item that is merely about the same topic as the task is not evidence. # Decision procedure Apply the steps in order and stop at the first that matches. 1. Find the divergence. It is the first turn where the memory run departs from the run without memory in way that leads to the failure. 2. If neither e1 nor e2 holds for that divergence, the label is E. 3. If the item the agent followed states something false about this environment, or prescribes rule that hurts in the very tasks it claims to cover, the label is A. 4. If the item the agent followed is sound, but memory also held another item that fits this task better and, followed instead, would have avoided the divergence, the label is D. 5. If the item is sound where it came from but its stated or implied scope does not cover this task, the label is B. 6. If its scope covers this task and the agent misread it, applied it to steps it does not cover, or let it push aside requirement the task states, the label is C. When several items are involved, label by the one that most directly produced the divergence and list the others too. # Labels The examples come from ScienceWorld. The labels apply to every benchmark in the same way. - A, wrong or harmful item. This includes an item distilled from failed run that generalizes wrong diagnosis. sound item used on the wrong task is or D, not A. Example: "interpret bulb behavior with caution" makes the agent hunt for circuit faults after correct negative reading, until the game clock runs out. - B, sound item outside its scope. This includes an item written for another task type and applied here, when no other item in memory covers this task better. An item whose scope covers the task is C, not B. Example: melting-point items that say "wait for plateau" applied to threshold task, so the agent keeps waiting after the answer is known. - C, sound and applicable item that was misused. This includes procedure adopted as the whole plan that drops the task's own first step. wrong item is A, not C. Example: circuit workflow copied step by step that skips the `focus on` step the task requires. - D, better item was passed over. sections.title: E How WikiTrace Uses Its Evidence
sections.content: E.1 Descent Judge The judge behind Figures 8 and 9 reads one WikiTrace run in text-world benchmark and labels every descent in it, where descent is stretch of consecutive memory calls that opens compilation or raw run and ends at the next game action. It receives the system prompt of Figure 21 and three user messages: the insights the agent saw, the agents full transcript with each descent marked, and the prompt of one axis (Figures 22 and 23). Each axis is separate call. The trigger and the target are read from the agents reasoning before the descent, and the effect from what the agent does after it. Every label carries verbatim quote from the agents messages, and checker sends an answer back once if quote is not found there. gpt-5.6-sol labels the trigger and the target, and GLM-5.3 labels them too, agreeing at Cohens κ of 0.77 and 0.63. The two judges agree on the effect only at κ = 0.46, so the effect label is the majority of these two and Claude Opus 5.5 (Fleiss κ = 0.49). All three judges run at medium reasoning effort. Of the 508 descents, 46 have no majority. The judges label 508 descents in the 430 descending runs; one descent has no trigger or target because its answer failed the checker twice. The prompt calls blocked attempt setback; the other labels in the text are the prompts codes. E.2 How Descent Helps We read pairs of episodes, WikiTrace and Insights Only on the same task and trial, whose outcomes differ, and give revise insight in ScienceWorld and new fact in ALFWorld (Figure 24). System prompt of the descent judge You code one aspect of why and how an LLM agent consulted its memory of past runs while playing text game. That aspect, the axis, is given in the last message, after the transcript. ## The agent and its memory The agent plays one text game episode: an ALFWorld household task, ScienceWorld science task, or PlanCraft crafting task. Its memory holds three levels built from earlier runs on other tasks: - insights: short lessons, each naming the run it came from as its source. All insights are in the agent's first message. - compilations: one summary per past run. - raw runs: the full log of each past run (its actions, observations and the agent's reasoning). The agent can list run's actions, read its turns, read files, or grep across runs. The first message also lists few past runs as similar to the current task. ## What you receive 1. Insights the agent saw: the insights block of the agent's first message, shared by every case of the same benchmark and trial. 2. The transcript: the agent's own context, unclipped. It starts with the agent's system prompt, then every message in order, numbered `-- message - <role> --`. In an agent message, `thinking ` is its private reasoning, `text ` is text it wrote, and `call #n ` is tool call. Each call's result follows as its own message. Game actions are `act` or `take_action` calls; every other call reads the memory. In message 0 the insights are replaced by pointer to item 1. 3. Burst marks. burst is one stretch of consecutive memory calls that opens past runs: it starts at the first call that opens compilation or raw run and ends at the agent's next game action or message. `======== BURST START ========` and `======== BURST END ========` mark each burst. Under each START line, bracketed line computed from the calls lists the runs the burst opens, with their outcomes, and the insights whose source is one of those runs. 4. The axis: its codes, how to decide among them, and the evidence to give. Read the whole transcript. Code every marked burst, in order, on this axis alone. ## Evidence For each burst give one verbatim quote and the number of the agent message it comes from. Copy the quote exactly, at least 12 characters, from single message. Return only the JSON object the schema asks for, with one entry per marked burst, in order. Figure 21: Descent judge system prompt. The insights, the transcript and one axis prompt (Figures 22 and 23) follow as three user messages. 27 Axis prompts: trigger and target ## Axis: trigger, why the agent opened past runs at this point Code the reason the agent states for opening the runs, in the message that makes the burst's first opening call and the messages before it. code definition against its nearest neighbour --------- setback An observation in this episode blocked or contradicted the agent's plan, and the agent treats it as problem: an action failed or had no effect, result differed from what the agent expected, search in the game found nothing, or needed item turned out to be missing. Against open question: there is concrete observation that the agent names as the problem. Uncertainty about the next step with nothing gone wrong is open question, and so is result the agent does not treat as problem. insight doubt The agent questions whether an insight holds, because two insights disagree or because the insight came from failed run, and opens runs to settle it. Against failed precedent: the agent names an insight, or says the insights disagree, and questions whether it holds. Mentioning an insight without questioning it is not insight doubt. Opening failed run only because it failed, with no doubted insight, is failed precedent. failed precedent past run listed as similar to the current task failed, and the agent opens it to avoid repeating that failure; nothing has gone wrong in its own episode. Against routine check: the opened run is failed run and the agent says it wants to avoid what went wrong there. open question The agent names one specific thing it does not know about its next step, and nothing has gone wrong. Against routine check: the agent states specific question or names alternatives. general wish to see how run did the task is routine check. routine check The agent opens run that matches its task, usually successful one, to see how that run did it, as precaution and without stated problem or question. The default when none of the above applies. Use the order setback > insight doubt > failed precedent > open question > routine check only when the agent gives two reasons. ## Fields - code: the trigger code. - quote and msg: the agent's own words (thinking or text) that show why it opened the runs, and their message number. - note: one sentence on how you decided. ## Axis: target, what the agent was looking for in the runs it opened Code what the agent says it wants from the runs, in the message that makes the burst's first opening call and the messages before it. If its thinking and its text differ, follow its thinking. code definition against its nearest neighbour --------- workaround way past something that blocks the agent: another way to make or obtain what it needs, where missing item can be found, or how another run got past the same block. Often searched for by content across runs, because no listed run is known to cover it. Against specific fact: workaround search is open-ended, looking for any run that might show way through. search that names one question to answer is specific fact, even when it looks across many runs. failure cause What went wrong in failed past run. Against workaround: the agent wants the failure explained, not way out of its own block. If its own episode is already blocked and it asks how the failed run got past the same block, use workaround. Against specific fact: opening the failed run an insight came from to ask whether the insight holds is specific fact; asking what went wrong in that run is failure cause. specific fact The answer to one named question: how command is written, whether something works or is needed, whether an insight holds, how result appears, or how the game behaves. Against procedure: it is driven by one question. Reading whole sequence with one part singled out stays procedure. procedure The working sequence of run: the order of its actions, often with where things were found. The default for reading run to reproduce its steps. If the agent names two targets: workaround > failure cause > specific fact > procedure. ## Fields - code: the target code. - quote and msg: the agent's own words, or memory call, that show what it looked for, and their message number. - note: one sentence on how you decided. Figure 22: Descent judge axis prompts for trigger and target, each sent in its own call. 28 Axis prompt: effect ## Axis: effect, how the opened runs affected the agent's next actions Find each point where the agent draws on the opened runs after this burst's END and before the next START, or the transcript's end: it says it took information from them, or acts on information only they supply. Code its adopted interpretation, including mistaken interpretations, not thoughts it rejects. Use need not succeed. The baseline is all insights, the current system prompt and its examples, the task, observations available before this burst even if first noticed through run, the stated plan, and information adopted from earlier bursts. Earlier mention alone does not establish adoption. The system prompt printed at the start of an opened run's log is baseline only insofar as its information was already available. Compare only against the insights the agent names, in thinking or text, from the start of the episode to the deciding point, and the insights listed under this burst's START line as sourced from the opened runs; do not search the other insights. Compare the specific information used, not merely the action's general purpose. Do not attribute discoveries from current game results to the run. Respect each insight's conditions and scope. code definition against its nearest neighbour --------- revise insight Because of the run, the agent acts on correction to an applicable insight's rule, condition or scope, or acts otherwise than that insight directs. Against confirm plan and refine insight: check every insight in that set, not only the one followed. Revision takes priority even if another insight states the chosen action and the displaced insight does not rule it out. Choosing between conflicting prescriptions is revision. refine insight The agent uses run-supplied detail about step an insight addresses, or uses the run to settle an unresolved choice among its listed options. Against revise insight: no applicable insight directs otherwise. Against confirm plan: refine insight only if the insight leaves something open that the agent must decide (which object, where, in what order, what value, how command is written) and the agent decides it from the run; if the insight already fixes it, confirm plan. fact true only of the opened run's episode is not detail unless the agent shows it also holds in this episode. choice already settled by the baseline, or an option demonstrated in the current system examples, is baseline. new fact The agent uses run-supplied information absent from the baseline about step no insight addresses. Against refine insight: identify the step, not merely the broad task. If an insight addresses that step and the run supplies its missing detail, use refine insight. confirm plan The agent explicitly says the run agrees with its plan or an insight, and the information taken is already in the baseline. Against none: matching actions alone do not establish stated agreement. Against revise insight: conflicting applicable prescription takes priority. none No qualifying run-derived use or explicit confirmation occurs. Includes rejected or unused information, and baseline-only use without stated agreement. Code every qualifying point and give the burst the highest: revise insight > refine insight > new fact > confirm plan > none. ## Fields - code: the effect code. - quote and msg: the agent's verbatim words or game action at the deciding point, and its message number. For none, quote its rejection or next game action. - note: one sentence identifying the information used and its baseline relationship; name the relevant insight when revising or refining. Figure 23: Descent judge axis prompt for effect. 29 Revise Insight (success) ScienceWorld, trial 0 Insights Only WikiTrace TASK determine if unknown substance is electrically conductive, blue box if it is, orange box if not. Why Insights drawn from failed runs say to always put the switch in the circuit. Built that way, the circuit stays dark even without the substance, so the bulb cannot tell whether conducts. insight-0080 Use the switch to complete the circuit Wrong Always include the switch in series and turn it on. New Fact (success) ALFWorld unseen, trial 2 Insights Only WikiTrace TASK clean some cloth and put it in cabinet. Why The insight sends the agent to towel holder, where it finds handtowel.
